newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Inchcape saw many Bain suitors.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Inchcape saw many Bain suitors.

text.p: International trading group Inchcape, which on Tuesday announced the sale of its insurance broking unit Bain Hogg to U.S. group Aon Corp for 160 million stg, was approached by several insurance brokers interested in buying the subsidiary.

Inchcape chief executive Philip Cushing told Reuters in an interview that other firms in addition to Aon expressed an interest in buying Bain Hogg after the parent company said just three weeks ago that it would divest itself of the business by the end of the year with the most likely option a demerger.

Inchcape is to shoulder an exceptional loss of about 195 million stg from the sale to Aon, which was completed at four o'clock local time this morning, but believes it is extracting greater value from this form of divestment than from demerger.

Some analysts say the value of Bain Hogg at demerger would have been in the region of 130 million stg. Inchcape would have to have ploughed in 13 million stg to give it sufficient capital and restructuring Bain Hogg was going to cost 20 million stg.
The disposal of Bain Hogg follows the sale by Inchcape of its quality testing unit for 380 million stg announced earlier this month. Both were part of the group's efforts to cut debt.

The group's borrowings at the end of 1995 stood at a net level of 463 million stg. The net effect of the two transactions is to reduce the 74 percent gearing at the half year point to just five percent on a proforma basis.
"Now we get on with our business as an international distributor pure and simple for the future," said Cushing.

While the disposals give Inchcape a necessary injection of cash, they dilute group earnings. Both Bain Hogg and Inchcape Testing are businesses that generate operating profit at a much richer rate per pound of turnover than either motor trading or marketing, the parent's main activities.
